## Abstract

This second part of the session, following [Environmental conflicts](s_06a_Conflicts.html),
introduces methods for **accounting environmental stressors on the global level**,
including the distinction between production- and consumption-based statistics. In the
accompanying group work, you continue analysing the challenges facing your selected country or
region.

## 📊 Data sources for the figures

Every data figure in the lecture is built from **openly available data**, so you can pull the
same data for **your own country**.

| Figure in the lecture | Where the data come from |
|---|---|
| Exports by African and European countries (treemaps) | [Atlas of Economic Complexity](https://atlas.hks.harvard.edu/) [@growthlabatlas], goods exports by 4-digit product (HS 1992), 2024 |
| Physical trade balance by world region | [UN IRP Global Material Flows Database](https://www.materialflows.net/) ([background](https://www.resourcepanel.org/global-material-flows-database)), imports minus exports in tonnes |
| The European carbon footprint | Taken from @wood2020, who use EXIOBASE 3 |

::: {.callout-note}
## Want to rebuild the figures yourself?

The figures are drawn by the R script `accounting_02_figures.R` in the
[`analysis/` folder of the course repository](https://github.com/graebnerc/EcolEcon26/tree/main/analysis).
The [README](https://github.com/graebnerc/EcolEcon26/blob/main/analysis/README.md#session-6b-accounting-environmental-stressors)
explains how to run it. You are welcome to change the regions, the year or the grouping, or
to adapt the code for your own poster.
:::

## 🐍 Production- and consumption-based footprints for your country

The [**one-page EXIOBASE tutorial**](exiobase_python.qmd) shows how to compute
production-based and consumption-based CO₂ emissions for your country with Python,
in about twenty lines of code. If you would rather not write code, Our World in Data
shows [production- and consumption-based CO₂ emissions](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/production-vs-consumption-co2-emissions)
for almost every country. These numbers come from a different model (the Global Carbon Budget),
which also makes them a good second source to check your EXIOBASE results against.
after:06b-->

## 📚 Follow-up Reading

- @tukker2020 — a concise discussion of consumption-based and production-based
  accounting, as well as further alternatives.

### 🏆 Further readings

- @miller2009 — a widely used textbook on input-output analysis.
- @wood2020 — the authors use environmental input-output tables to describe the
  structure of greenhouse gas emissions of the European Union. They show that
  delineating an effective policy mix requires one to understand this structure,
  including the relative importance of imported emissions and sectoral heterogeneity.
